summary:
Malawi's Penal Code criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 153 covers carnal knowledge against the order of nature and permits up to fourteen years' imprisonment with or without corporal punishment, and section 154 punishes attempts with up to seven years on the same terms. Gross indecency between men, in public or private, is a felony carrying up to five years. Human Rights Watch reports the sections as exposing men to up to fourteen years and women to five.

On 28 June 2024 a three-member panel of the Constitutional Court dismissed the challenge to sections 153, 154 and 156, an application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani. The court held that the sections criminalise consensual same-sex conduct among other acts but do not discriminate against homosexual persons because they prohibit all people from certain conduct, and it rejected claims of discriminatory application, leaving any reform to parliament. Human Rights Watch called the ruling a dark day and warned of heightened risks of arbitrary arrest and violence.

Jana Gonani, a trans woman, was convicted under section 153(c) by a Magistrate's Court in Mangochi on 23 December 2021 and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment, served in a men's prison. Human Rights Watch reports that people whose gender expression differs from expectations are the most likely to be targeted under these provisions, so the sections reach gender identity directly in practice.

Enforcement is documented as arbitrary and violent. Human Rights Watch's 61-page report Let Posterity Judge, released on 26 October 2018 from interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre alongside lawyers, activists and officials, found that police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people and sometimes assaulted them. Medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds: a trans man was beaten and then refused treatment, and nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests.

A moratorium suspending arrests and prosecutions under sections 153 to 156 was announced by the attorney general on 5 November 2012 and reaffirmed in July 2014 and on 18 December 2015 by the justice minister. The High Court in Mzuzu granted an injunction on 9 February 2016 ordering police to resume arrests and annulled the moratorium on 19 February 2016 on the ground that the executive lacked constitutional authority to suspend parliamentary laws, leaving its legality contested. Police worked around it while it stood: in April 2018 officers in Mzuzu arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, and charged him under section 156 rather than section 153, apparently to circumvent the moratorium while both laws faced constitutional challenge.

Arrest itself carries a documented secondary risk. Two men arrested on 7 December 2015 on homosexuality charges, Cuthbert Kulemela and Kelvin Gonani, had their house ransacked and were assaulted by neighbours, threatened with being burned alive, subjected to attempted extortion and humiliated by community police through forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photographs distributed on social media.

A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex has no recognition to rely on. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, bans all same-sex marriages and unions, provides that gender is assigned at birth, and does not permit a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery to marry someone of that person's prior gender.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility has been voiced at the highest levels. In April 2010 President Bingu wa Mutharika called same-sex marriage evil and bad before the eyes of God, and in July 2011 he threatened activists Undule Mwakasungula and Gift Trapence that he would hunt them in their homes and smoke them out, forcing them into hiding amid treason threats. The 2011 US State Department human rights report found that senior officials created a discriminatory environment, citing tourism minister Daniel Liwimbi describing same-sex activity as very un-Malawian, and it recorded harsh prison conditions, discrimination against LGBT people and 20 deaths in the July 2011 protests.

Hostility has also come from party and religious figures. In January 2016 People's Party spokesperson Ken Msonda wrote on Facebook that gay people are worse than dogs and should be killed; the Malawi Law Society filed charges, but the director of public prosecution took over and discontinued the case on 21 January. The Muslim Association of Malawi called for the death penalty for gay people in February 2014, and on 4 January 2017 thousands across 28 districts marched against legalising homosexuality in protests led by the Episcopal Conference of Malawi and the Evangelical Association of Malawi. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests around the 2024 constitutional case, claiming it sought to legalise same-sex marriage.

Malawi has resisted external pressure rather than absorbed it. At the 2011 Universal Periodic Review the government rejected every recommendation to decriminalise same-sex relations, stating that it had no plans to legalize homosexuality and should not be unduly singled out and unnecessarily pressured; recommendations had come from Sweden, Mexico, France, Canada, Germany, Australia, the United Kingdom, Italy, Austria, Ireland, Luxembourg, the United States, Spain, Switzerland and Norway. The UN Human Rights Committee's June 2012 provisional concluding observations urged Malawi to amend the Penal Code and protect same-sex couples from violence, and the country has not filed its ICCPR report for over 17 years. Donor pressure is contested domestically: the Malawi Council of Churches urged international organisations to refrain from using aid as a means of forcing the country to legalise acts like homosexuality, and Justice Minister George Chaponda blamed civil society leaders for withdrawn foreign aid.

The government's own 2012 UN report describes a highly conservative society in which the vast majority of society has not accepted homosexuality and homosexuality is not practiced in the open. Community visibility exists but is fragile: the country's first pride parade was held in Lilongwe on 26 June 2021, organised by the Nyasa Rainbow Alliance with more than 50 attendees delivering a petition for marriage equality and healthcare. Public hostility attaches to visibility itself. Bail was denied to Tiwonge Chimbalanga and Steven Monjeza in 2009 because the public out there is angry with them, and the magistrate said he sentenced them to protect society; a January 2016 interview in which gay man Eric Sambisa said kill us or give us our rights led to his brief police detention and a period in hiding.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition. The Marriage, Divorce and Family Relations Law, in force from 17 April 2015, states that gender is assigned at birth and bars a person who has undergone gender reassignment surgery from marrying someone of that person's prior gender, while banning same-sex marriage and unions outright.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The only protection identified is limited and media-specific: since 2019 the Communications (Broadcasting) Regulations 2019, at sections 22(1-d) and 30(2-d), define hate messages to include speech degrading or inciting violence on grounds of gender identity and prohibit broadcast content likely to incite hatred on account of sexual preference or other status.

Trans residents have been prosecuted under the penal code. Tiwonge Chimbalanga, a trans woman, was arrested in Blantyre in late December 2009 after holding a traditional engagement ceremony with Steven Monjeza, found guilty on 18 May 2010 of unnatural offenses and indecent practices between males under sections 153 and 156, and sentenced to 14 years' imprisonment with hard labour before being pardoned by President Bingu wa Mutharika on 29 May 2010. International outlets covering the trial failed to report Chimbalanga's gender identity. Jana Gonani received eight years in December 2021.

Advocacy for services has produced limited official engagement. In September 2009 Mary Shawa, secretary for nutrition, HIV and AIDS in the president's office, argued that Malawi must give gay people access to HIV and AIDS services on a human rights approach for risk groups such as men who have sex with men, and CEDEP's Gift Trapence has contrasted arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. The June 2021 Lilongwe pride petition to city officials demanded better access to healthcare for LGBTQ people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No entry, visa or passport-marker rules for Malawi are sourced in this inventory, and no airport or border screening practice specific to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers is documented. Whether a trans visitor faces document inspection, secondary screening or outing at the border remains unresolved on the available material.

The inventory provides no violence figures for trans people in Malawi against which a general homicide rate could be set, so no comparative magnitude of trans-specific violence can be stated. The 2011 protest death toll of 20 is reported by a foreign government's human rights report without a stated relation to LGBT targeting, and that relation is unresolved here.

Whether parliament has taken up the reform the Constitutional Court left to it after 28 June 2024 is not sourced. Enforcement of the 2019 broadcasting hate-speech provisions, and whether any complaint under them has been pursued, is likewise not documented. The application of section 154 to gender-identity-related conduct is not evidenced in the inventory.
